name: Cynefin Framework
use_case: A sense-making framework for teams that cannot agree on how to tackle a problem because they disagree about what kind of problem it is. It sorts the situation into clear, complicated, complex or chaotic, and only then prescribes the response: apply best practice, bring in expert analysis, run small safe-to-fail experiments, or stabilise first and diagnose later. Best used when one group demands a detailed up-front plan while another wants to start experimenting, or when a proven best practice keeps failing because the situation is genuinely unpredictable rather than merely difficult.
strengths: stops teams applying best practice to problems that have none
gives permission to experiment when the answer is genuinely unknowable
explains why one team wants analysis and another wants to just try something
the chaotic domain justifies acting before understanding, which plans rarely allow
weaknesses: classification itself is contested and often argued longer than the problem
abstract enough that groups need a facilitator who has used it before
offers no concrete technique once the domain is named
misclassifying complex as complicated produces confident, wrong plans
use_cases: A health authority facing a fast-spreading outbreak must decide whether to act at once to contain it or first gather data, while its own experts disagree about how predictable the situation is.
A ministry is asked for a detailed multi-year implementation plan for a social problem where nobody can say in advance how families and services will respond to any intervention.

A leadership team keeps talking past each other about a stalled transformation programme and needs a shared way to tell which parts are routine, which need specialists and which are genuinely uncertain.

An IT operations group wants to sort its incident types into those a fixed runbook can handle, those that need a specialist's diagnosis, and those where the only way forward is to try small changes and watch.
